So, one may say that the prayers which are considered to be very efficacious, should be included in the first category of speech in which not only the meanings but the words also must be carefully safeguarded, for both are equally intended.

**Meanings and words, and the reporting of a hadith.**

Now, as for other kinds of speech in which it is the meanings that are really intended and not the words, the masters of the science of Hadith and the jurists in general believe that in such places words can be changed provided that the meaning does not suffer but remains in-tact. Most of the jurists and the masters of the science of Hadith, however, believe that although it is better to report a hadith as far as possible in exactly the same words as one has heard without making any change intentionally, yet if one cannot recall the exact words, it is also permissible to report the meaning in one's own words, and that the words of the hadith quoted above - "... conveyed it exactly as he had heard" - might also mean that one should report the meaning of a hadith exactly and without any alteration. But if one reads a very accurate translation of the Holy Qur'an or even an Arabic version in which the original words have been replaced by certain other words without injuring the sense, the Shari'ah shall not accept it as a recitation of the Holy Qur'an, and one will not get any reward of recitation for it. For, it is not the meanings alone which constitute the Holy Qur'an; "Qur'an" is the name of meanings inherent in the words revealed by Allah to the Holy Prophet so that the two are inseparable from each other.

**The punishment sent down from the heavens.**

Due to their actions He sent down a torment from the sky upon the wrongdoers among them, because they trespassed over the limits of the law and disobeyed His command. " This demonstrates the worst type of rebellion and disobedience, and it is why Allah released His anger and punishment upon them, all because of their sinning and defying His commands. Ad-Dahhak said that Ibn 'Abbas said, "Every word in Allah's Book that says Rijz means, 'a punishment.'" Mujahid, Abu Malik, As-Suddi, Al-Hasan and Qatadah were reported to have said that Rijz means 'Torment.' Ibn Abi Hatim narrated that Sa'd bin Malik, Usamah bin Zayd and Khuzaymah bin Thabit said that the Messenger of Allah said,. Then the evildoers substituted a saying other than that which had been said to them; so We sent down upon the evildoers wrath from the heaven for their wickedness. They could neither ward off the opening of heaven above them with their stratagems nor avert the cords of affliction below them by relying on their usual states. They gnashed the teeth of remorse when the fangs of pain bit them. How could this have benefited them when the situation was hopelessḍ. They were given possession of a great city and told to enter it—not in a vainglorious manner—but in humility and repentance; but instead they started rejoicing in their victory. They should have shown their gratitude by remaining obedient to Him, but they did quite the opposite.

60.text:
The verses before this have been about what was sent down to the people, and this one is about what was struck out of a stone for them, and it ends on what they were told not to do with it. "And remember when Moses prayed for water for his people, We said" opens on an asking and on an answer in one clause, and the asking is put first, with the people named as the ones the water was for, so the prayer is described as being for them and not for himself. "Strike the rock with your staff" is the answer, and it is short, a single act with a single thing in the hand, and the striking is stopped at, since the water could have come without it and the act was put there so that there would be a share of effort in what was given. "Then twelve springs gushed out" gives what came of it, and the number is the number of the tribes, so the water is shared out before anyone shares it, and the gushing is described as coming out of the stone rather than as being drawn up from a well. "and each tribe knew its drinking place" is the second half of the same provision, and the knowing is what keeps the twelve springs from being a matter of dispute, since each tribe had its own place and did not have to travel or to go against the others for it. "We then said" turns the verse from the water to the word that came with it, and the word is put after the giving and not before it. "Eat and drink of Allah's provisions" names both the food and the water in one clause, and the eating and drinking are without effort or work, the provisions already provided and already there. "and do not go about spreading corruption in the land" is the one thing asked of them in return, and it is not a new command but the shape the being grateful takes, since the disorder named here is disobedience after a blessing, and the land is the land the water and the food were given in. The verse after this turns from the provision to what was asked of them when they had it.

**Moses prayed for water, and the prayer asked for in a drought.**

And mention when Moses sought water for his people for they suffered thirst in the wilderness We said ‘Strike with your staff the rock the one that ran off with his robe a light cube-like rock about the size of a man’s head made of marble and he struck it and there exploded there burst and gushed forth from it twelve fountains equal to the number of tribes each people each tribe among them came to know their drinking-place which they did not share with any of the others. Remember, from Allah’s blessings upon you, when you were in the wilderness, and you suffered great thirst, so Moses prayed to his Lord and asked that He give you water. Parched with thirst, they requested Sayyidna Musa 1t to pray to Allah for water. Allah said, "Remember My favor on you when I answered the supplication of your Prophet, Musa, when he asked Me to provide you with water. It has been asked whether it is necessary, in times of drought, to offer formal prayers in order to beseech Allah for rains. The present verse tells us that Sayyidna Musa just prayed for water, and Allah made a miraculous provision. It shows that the essential thing in beseeching Allah for rains is just a prayer. No matter what form the prayer takes, all the scholars agree that it cannot be effective unless it is accompanied by a repentance for one's sins, a confession of one's powerlessness, a sincere expression of humility and an affirmation of servitude to Allah.

**Strike the rock with your staff.**

Ibn 'Abbas said that the Children of Israel, "Had a square stone that Musa was commanded to strike with his staff and, as a result, twelve springs burst out of that stone, three on each side. This in order for Moses to work with his self nafs in mov ing the stone and give him responsibility in striking it with his staff. Thus there would be a measure of [human] effort involved in making His decree come to pass when he sought water for his people. When Allah has given a certain stone the unusual property of drawing iron to itself, it cannot be, logically and rationally speaking, impossible that He should also give another stone the property of absorbing water from the earth and of releasing it again. Otherwise, it is in no way impossible that Allah should produce water within a stone itself. I made the water available for you, making it gush out through a stone.

**Twelve springs gushed out of the rock.**

It had 12 nipples that resemble the nipples of women and upon striking each one of these a spring gushed therefrom. Allah commanded that he hit the rock with his stick, and when he hit it, twelve springs appeared from it, the same number as the number of your tribes. Twelve springs burst out of that stone, a designated spring for each of your tribes. (And there gushed forth out of it twelve springs)(7:160), describing what first occurred when the water begins to gush out. In the Ayah in Surat Al-Baqarah, Allah described what happened later on, meaning when the water burst out in full force.

**Each tribe knew its drinking place.**

Water gushed from them, and Allah made clear to each tribe which was their spring to drink from, so that there would be no conflict between you. Each tribe was, therefore, designated a certain spring, and they used to drink from their springs. They never had to travel from their area, they would find the same bounty in the same manner they had in the first area."This narration is part of the long Hadith that An-Nasa'i, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim recorded about the trials. He singled out for each tribe a marker by which they would know their drinking place so that they would not go to each others' drinking places. The drinking places are different and each comes to their own so one drinking place is sweet and fresh another salty and bitter another clear and pure and another dried up with only a few drops. Then the Real wanted each people to follow a way sunna stick to their boundary ḥadd and not dispute with their companions.

**Eat and drink of Allah's provisions.**

the honey and quails (and drink of) all the springs (that which Allah hath provided. And do not act corruptly, making mischief in the earth) and do not cause mischief on the earth, or act contrary to what Moses commanded. And He told you to eat and drink from what He provided for you, without any effort or work from you, and told you not to put your efforts into ruining things on earth. You eat from the manna and the quails and drink from the water that I provided for you, without any effort or hardship for you. What they have been asked to eat is the Mann and the Salwa (manna and quails), and the water is, of course, the one which had come out of the rock.

**Do not spread corruption in the land.**

The Israelites have, in this verse, been asked not to spread disorder which in this context signifies disobedience to Allah and transgression of His Commandments. (And do not act corruptly, making mischief on the earth) meaning, "Do not return the favor by committing acts of disobedience that cause favors to disappear." And We said to them ‘Eat and drink of that which God has provided and do not be degenerate in the earth seeking corruption’ mufsidīn is a circumstantial qualifier emphasising its operator the subject of the verb lā ta‘thaw ‘do not be degenerate’ derived from ‘athiya meaning afsada ‘to corrupt’. When He had met their needs He bid them to be grateful to preserve the command and to stop choosing sin and so He said and do not be degenerate in the earth seeking corruption.

61.text:
The provision of the last verse is what this one turns on, and the turning is a want. "And remember when you said, O Moses" opens on the people speaking again, and the speech is put in the same form as the demand in the verse about seeing Allah, an address to Moses with what they want in it. "We cannot endure the same meal every day" is the complaint itself, and it is not about hunger but about one kind of food, since the meal they cannot endure is the one that came down to them without work, the manna and the quails, and what they are tired of is the sameness of it rather than the want of it. "So just call upon your Lord on our behalf" is the asking that follows the complaint, and the wording puts the prayer on Moses and not on themselves, with the Lord named as his Lord rather than as theirs, which is the first sign of how far they had gone from it. "He will bring forth for us some of what the earth produces of herbs, cucumbers, garlic, lentils, and onions" is what they want in place of it, and the list is a list of things that grow in the ground and are got by work, so the exchange they are asking for is from a food that came down to a food that comes up, and the five things named are the diet of the life they used to live. "Moses scolded them" is the answer, and it is short, and the scolding is put before the words so that the reply is known as a turning on them and not as a ruling. "Do you exchange what is better for what is worse" is the question the rebuke takes the shape of, and the two sides of the exchange are named only as better and worse, without the food being repeated, so the question is about the choosing and not about the things chosen. "You can go down to any village and you will find what you have asked for" gives them what they asked for and takes away the thing they had, since the going down is a leaving of the place they were in and of the provision that came with it, and the finding is put as certain. "They were stricken with disgrace and misery" turns from the food to what settled on them, and the two are named as a striking and not as a falling, so the disgrace is described as something put on them and stamped on them rather than as something that grew out of their state. "and they invited the displeasure of Allah for rejecting Allah's signs and unjustly killing the prophets" gives the reason, and the reason is two things rather than one, the signs rejected and the prophets killed, with the killing named as unjust so that no reading of it can make it a punishing of a crime. "This is a fair reward for their disobedience and violations" closes the verse on the shape of the answer, and the two words at the end are the general form of the two things named, since disobedience is doing what is prohibited and violation is going past the limit set, and the reward is called fair because it answers both.

**The manna and the quails, and the want of something else.**

Also, remember when you were ungrateful for the blessings of your Lord, and became tired of the manna and quails He sent down to you, and said that you would not put up with one type of food. " Al-Hasan Al-Basri said about the Children of Israel, "They were bored and impatient with the type of food they were provided. Divine provision was given to them in the form of manna and quails so that, free from the struggle for a livelihood, they would be able to devote themselves entirely to carrying out God’s commandments; but they took to demanding spicy, cooked foods instead. Discontented with the basic necessities of life, they sought to indulge in worldly luxury.

**Herbs, cucumbers, garlic, lentils, and onions.**

And when you said Moses we will not endure one sort of food; pray to your Lord for us that He may bring forth for us of what the earth pro duces-green herbs cucumbers garlic lentils onions ; He said Would you exchange what is better with what is lowlierḍ Go down to a city you shall have what you demanded ; And abasement and wretchedness were cast upon them and they incurred God's wrath; that was because they used to disbe lieve the signs of God and slay prophets without right; that was because they disobeyed and they were transgressors. They also remembered the life they used to live, when their diet consisted of lentils, onions, garlic and herbs. (Its Fum), "Ibn 'Abbas said that Fum means, garlic." He also said that the expression, 'Fumu-lanna' means, 'bake for us', according to the languages of old. Ibn Jarir commented, "If this is true, then 'Fum' is one of the words whose pronounciation were altered, the letter 'fa' was replaced by the letter 'tha', since they are similar in sound.

**Do you exchange what is better for what is worse.**

Moses (said: Would you exchange that which is higher) i.e. that which is better and more honourable: honey and quails (for that which is lower) that which is much worse: lentils and onions? Moses said, disapproving of your request, that you wanted to exchange manna and quails which were better and nobler and came to you without effort or work, for what was lesser and worse. They were not content with the goodness of [God] choosing for them nor were they patient in His managing what He desired for them in basic food and clothing. (Go down to any city) where you came from; and it is also said that this means any city, (thus you shall get that which you demand) what you have requested is to be found there. You were told to go down from this land to any town, and that you would find what you had asked for in its fields and markets. (Go you down to any Misr) means, 'any city', as Ibn 'Abbas said. In their confusion they fell back to their customary behavior of eating impure food and finding contentment in a lower state so He returned them to the suffering of ignominy muqāsāt al-hawān and bound them to perpetual disappointment idāmat al-khidhlān.

**Stricken with disgrace and misery.**

As to how the Companions, their successors and the great commentators have interpreted the disgrace and degradation which has settled on the Jews, let us present a summary in the words of Ibn Kathir: "No matter how wealthy they grow, they will always be despised by other people; whoever gets hold of them will humiliate them, and attach to them the emblems of servitude. " The commentator Dahhak Ibn Muzahim reports from the blessed Companion Abdullah Ibn Abbas that the Jews will always remain under the domination of others, will be paying taxes and tributes to them - that is to say, they will themselves never have power and authority in the real sense of the term. " Also, Abu Al-'Aliyah, Ar-Rabi' bin Anas and As-Suddi said that 'misery' used in the Ayah means, 'poverty.' 'Atiyah Al-'Awfi said that 'misery' means, 'paying the tilth .' In addition, Ad-Dahhak commented on Allah's statement,. (and they drew on themselves the wrath of Allah) means, "They went back with the wrath. (And humiliation) the capitation tax (and wretchedness) the attire of poverty (were stamped upon them) were imposed on them (and they were visited with wrath from Allah) as they deserved to be forsaken by Allah. Due to following whims and repeatedly turning away from what Allah chose for them, they were disgraced, given poverty and misery.

**The rope from Allah, and the rope from men.**

Now, the 'rope' or means from Allah refers to the case of those whom Allah Himself has, through His own commandment, saved from this disgrace - for example, children, women, or those who are totally devoted to prayer and worship and never go to war against Muslims. The 'rope' or means from men refers to a treaty of peace with the Muslims, or a permission to live in a Muslim country on payment of the Jizyah (the tax levied on non-Muslims living in a Muslim country, which exonerates them from military service etc.) Since the Holy Qur'an uses the expression "from men" and not "from Muslims", a third situation is also possible - the Jews may make political arrangements with other non-Muslims, live under their backing and protection, and thus be in 'peace'. Another verse of the Holy Qur'an also speaks of the disgrace of the Jews, but with some addition: Allah had made it quite clear to the Jews through Sayyidna Musa (Moses) that if they con-tinued to be disobedient, they would always have to live under the domination of other nations. Says the Holy Qur'an: ‌ "And when your Lord proclaimed He would send forth against them, unto the Day of Resurrection, those who should visit them with evil chastisement.

**Rejecting the signs, killing the prophets, and the reward for it.**

(That was because they used to disbelieve in the Ayat (proofs, evidences, etc.) of Allah and killed the Prophets wrongfully.) means, "This is what We rewarded the Children of Israel with: humiliation and misery. (That) being forsaken by Allah and visited by humiliation and wretchedness (was because they disbelieved in Allah's revelations) they disbelieved in Muhammad ﷺ and in the Qur'an (and slew the prophets wrongfully) without any right and for no crime whatsoever. They earned Allah’s anger, because they turned away from His religion, and disbelieved His signs, and unjustly and brutally killed His prophets – all because they rebelled against Allah and used to transgress His limits. They went so far as to shed the blood of prophets and violated the sanctity of [God's] command with their lack of shame. So hardened did they become that even clear signs of God could not move their hearts. They opposed and even killed those servants of God who sought to admonish them. (That was because they disobeyed and used to transgress the bounds) mentions another reason why the Children of Israel were punished in this manner, for they used to disobey and transgress the limits. Disobedience is to do what is prohibited, while transgression entails overstepping the set limits of what is allowed and what is prohibited. (That) Allah's wrath (was for their disobedience) on the Sabbath (and transgression) slaying the prophets and declaring transgressions to be lawful. When sincere counsel naṣīḥa did not succeed with them retribution and humiliation faḌīḥa overtook them. It is said that the children of Israel were divided in their aspirations and scattered in their objectives.

62.text:
After the long account of the people of the last verses, this one steps back and lays down a rule that is not about them alone. "Indeed, the believers, Jews, Christians, and Sabians" puts four names in a row, and the first of them is the name the believers in Muhammad are called by, while the other three are the names of communities that had a prophet and a book before him, so the verse is not a list of paths that all lead to the same place but a list of the people who followed a messenger in his own time. The fourth name is the one that is least settled, and the commentators differ over who the Sabians were, some putting them between two of the known religions and some taking them for a people with a book of their own, so the list does not close on a name that everyone can place. "whoever truly believes in Allah and the Last Day and does good will have their reward with their Lord" is the rule, and it turns on the word whoever, since the four names before it are the groups the rule is spoken about and not the ground of it, the ground being belief in Allah and in the Last Day with good done along with them. Two articles of faith are named here and no more, and the two are the first and the last of the creed, so naming them is a way of naming all of it, since nothing between the two can be had without them. The reward is put with their Lord rather than in a place or a thing, and the good that is asked for is the good that follows belief and not a good that stands without it. "And there will be no fear for them" takes away the first of the two things a person waits for, which is what is coming, and "nor will they grieve" takes away the second, which is what has gone, so the two together cover the whole of a life looked at from its end, the fear of what is ahead and the grief over what is behind. The verse names no community in either of the two clauses, and the promise is not given to a group but to whoever meets the condition, which is why the naming of the Muslims along with the others is not an extension of the invitation but a sign that the rule has always been one rule, and that no community has a standing with Allah that another does not have.

**The believers, the Jews, the Christians, and the Sabians.**

Surely those who believe who believed before in the prophets and those of Jewry the Jews and the Christians and the Sabaeans a Christian or Jewish sect whoever from among them believes in God and the Last Day in the time of our Prophet and performs righteous deeds according to the Law given to him — their wage that is the reward for their deeds is with their Lord and no fear shall befall them neither shall they grieve the singular person of the verbs āmana ‘believes’ and ‘amila ‘performs’ takes account of the singular form of man ‘whoever’ but in what comes afterwards of the plural pronouns its plural meaning is taken into account. Muslims, who are the followers of the Prophet Muhammad; Jews who follow the Prophet Moses; Christians, who follow the Prophet Jesus; and Sabeans, who adhered to the teachings of John the Baptist, the Prophet Yahya. The Jews are the followers of Prophet Musa, who used to refer to the Tawrah for judgment. Those who have faith from the nation of Muhammad ﷺ and from the communities who came before him – from the Jews, the Christians and Sabians (said to be a group who followed prophets who were of the faith of Abraham, peace be upon him) – will have their reward with their Lord. (and those who are Jews) who deviated from the religion of Moses, (and Christians) those who became Christians (and Sabaeans) a Christian sect whose members shave the middle of their heads, read the Gospel, worship the angels and say: Now, this account may lead the listeners, or the Jews themselves, to suppose that, in view of such transgression, their Taubah (repentance), if they agree to offer it, would not be acceptable to Allah. In order to dispel such a misgiving, the present verse lays down a general principle: no matter how a man has been behaving earlier, so long as he submits himself fully to the commandments of Allah in his beliefs and in his deeds both, he is acceptable to Allah, and will get his reward.

**Why each name is used, and who the Sabians are.**

This indicates that they were called Yahud, because they repented and because they were kind to each other. Abu 'Amr bin Al-'Ala' said that they were called Yahud, because they swayed when they read the Tawrah. It was said that they were called 'Nasara', because they inhabited a land called An-Nasirah (Nazareth), as Qatadah, Ibn Jurayj and Ibn 'Abbas were reported to have said, Allah knows best. The Ummah of Muhammad was called 'Mu'minin' (believers), because of the depth of their faith and certainty, and because they believe in all of the previous Prophets and matters of the Unseen. There is a difference of opinion over the identity of the Sabians. It appears that the closest opinion to the truth, and Allah knows best, is Mujahid's statement and those who agree with him like Wahb bin Munabbih, that the Sabians are neither Jews nor Christians nor Majus nor polytheists. This is why the idolators used to call whoever embraced Islam a 'Sabi', meaning, that he abandoned all religions that existed on the earth.

**Why the Muslims are named along with them.**

One might also ask why the verse mentions the Muslims, for if it is an invitation to Islam, there is no need to extend the invitation to those who have already accepted Islam. But if we keep in mind the richly concentrated style of the Holy Qur'an, and try to look beyond the literal sense of the words into the implications and suggestions contained in the verse, we would find that the inclusion of the Muslim factor has added a new dimension to the meaning. But the suggestion contained in such a formulation is that the favours of the king do not proceed from any personal attachment to the friends, but depend on the quality of obedience and loyalty, and hence the foes too will become worthy of his favours if they acquire the necessary quality. This is the raison d'etre of mentioning the Muslims along with the non-Muslims in this verse, which should never be taken to imply that salvation can be attained without accepting Islam. Here the Muslims have not been mentioned separately, but have been grouped with other communities associated with prophets. But God does not have a special relationship with any particular community. In the Hereafter, people will be judged according to their deeds and character, and not on the basis of the group to which they belong.

**Two articles of faith, named first and last.**

The verse mentions only two articles of faith of the Islamic creed -- faith in Allah and faith in the Day of Judgment. This should not be taken to mean that in order to attain salvation it is enough to have faith only in Allah and in the Day of Judgment. For, the Holy Qur'an repeatedly declares that he who does not believe in the prophets, in angels and in the Books of Allah is not a Muslim. Faith in Allah is the first article in the Islamic creed, while faith in the Day of Judgment is the last. By mentioning only these two, the verse intends to say in a succinct manner that it is necessary to have faith in all the articles of the creed, from the first to the last. Moreover, it is through the prophets and the Books of Allah alone that man can acquire any knowledge of the essence and the attributes of Allah and of what is to happen on the Day of Judgment, while the Books of Allah are revealed to the prophets through an angel. So, it is not possible to have faith in Allah and the Day of Judgment until and unless one has faith in the angels, in the Books of Allah and in the prophets.

**Whoever truly believes, and does good.**

" our hearts have returned (saba'at) unto Allah " , (whoever believeth) from amongst them (in Allah and the Last Day and does right) in that which is between them and their Lord, (surely their reward is with their Lord, and there shall no fear come upon them neither shall they grieve). Then He said whoever believes meaning if they fear [God] in [their] different ways of knowing [Him] all of them will have a beautiful place of return and an ample reward. For anyone who affirms the Real in His signs and believes in what He has said concerning His truth and attributes the dissimilarity of [religious] laws and diversity that occurs in [the] name[s] [of religion] is not a problem in terms of who merits [God's] good pleasure. This statement by Ibn 'Abbas indicates that Allah does not accept any deed or work from anyone, unless it conforms to the Law of Muhammad that is, after Allah sent Muhammad . It is obvious enough that after the revelation of the Holy Qur'an, which is the last message of Allah, perfect obedience to Allah can only mean accepting Islam and following the Last Prophet Muhammad 23 The verse, in effect, assures everyone that once a man has accepted Islam, all his former transgressions, whether in the matter of beliefs or in that of deeds, will be forgiven, and he will become worthy of receiving the rewards of the other world. When Allah sent Muhammad as the Last and Final Prophet and Messenger to all of the Children of Adam, mankind was required to believe in him, obey him and refrain from what he prohibited them; those who do this are true believers. When Salman related to the Prophet, Allah bless him and give him peace, the story of the monks, the Prophet told him that they will dwell in hell fire . When Salman went to see the Messenger of Allah, Allah bless him and give him peace, he informed him about their worship and striving. They used to pray and fast; they believed in you and bore witness that you will be sent as a prophet .

**No fear for them, nor will they grieve.**

It is said that this means that no fear will come upon them concerning torment in the future life nor will they grieve about anything they have left behind. And it is also said that this means: they shall have no fear when death is slain and hell is closed. They will not fear what awaits them in the Afterlife, nor grieve over what happened to them on earth. (No doubt! Verily, the Awliya' of Allah, no fear shall come upon them nor shall they grieve)(10:62). For anyone who is in His protection it is fitting that no fear shall befall them neither shall they grieve. The diversity of [religious] paths in spite of the unity of the source does not prevent a goodly acceptance [for all].

63.text:
The mountain over the heads of a people is the image this verse leaves, and the verse is about what was asked of them under it. "And remember when We took a covenant from you and raised the mountain above you saying" joins two things that are usually kept apart, a covenant taken and a mountain lifted, and the joining is the point, since the covenant is the same one the verses before have been going over and the mountain is what made the taking of it something seen rather than something agreed to in words. The word saying is put before the speech and not after it, so what follows is the wording of the covenant itself, the two being given as one event and not as a promise and then a threat. "Hold firmly to that Scripture which We have given you and observe its teachings so perhaps you will become mindful of Allah" is that wording, and it has three parts in it. The holding firmly is the first, and it is not a taking but a keeping hold of something already given, which is why the Scripture is named as a thing We have given you and not as a thing being sent down at that moment. The observing of its teachings is the second part, and it is kept separate from the holding, since a book can be kept and not followed, so the verse asks for the keeping and for the doing along with it. The third part is the end the two are for, and it is put as a perhaps rather than as a result, so mindfulness is what the holding and the observing may bring and not a thing they settle by themselves. Nothing in the wording is about the mountain, and the mountain is not made into the reason for the covenant, which is the reading the verse closes off.

**A covenant taken, and the mountain raised above them.**

And mention when We made a covenant with you your pledge to act according to what is in the Torah and We had raised above you the Mount which We uprooted from the earth and placed above you when you refused to accept it sc. the Torah and We said ‘Take forcefully seriously and with effort what We have given you and remember what is in it acting in accordance with it so that you might preserve yourselves’ from the Fire or acts of disobedience. Allah then mentions the covenant He undertook with them, saying (And when We made a covenant with you) took your consent (and caused the Mount to tower above you) pulled out and fixed high above your heads the mountain for taking the covenant: Allah reminded the Children of Israel of the pledges, covenants and promises that He took from them to believe in Him alone, without a partner, and follow His Messengers. Allah stated that when He took their pledge from them, He raised the mountain above their heads, so that they affirm the pledge that they gave Allah and abide by it with sincerity and seriousness. Remember when Allah made a contract with you: that you should have faith in Allah and His prophets. A covenant was made with Moses’ people that they would faithfully carry out the divine teachings given to them in the form of the Ten Commandments. Having received the Torah from Allah, Sayyidna Musa (Moses) returned from Mount Tur (Sinai) and recited it to the Israelites.

**Seventy men selected, and the mountain hung over their heads.**

To begin with, they replied that they would not obey the injunctions until and unless Allah Himself told them that it was His book. Seventy men, as we have related above, were selected to go to Mount Tur and to hear Allah attest the authenticity of the Torah. On their re-turn, they bore witness to the Torah being a Book of Allah, but added something on their own to what Allah had actually said. In reply to this insolence, Allah commanded the angels to raise Mount Tur and let it hang in the air above their heads as a threat that if they did not fulfill their covenant with Allah, it would fall on them and crush them. The Israelites, then, had no choice but to submit. The Talmud tells how, at this time, God turned a mountain upside down, holding it above them and told them either to accept the teachings of the Torah, or be destroyed there and then. There is no proof more powerful than the eyewitnessing of the mount Ṭūr He raised above them which was a mountain jabal but they lacked the light of inner sight baṣīra and so the witnessing of physical vision baṣar did not benefit them. (And (remember) when We raised the mountain over them as if it had been a canopy, and they thought that it was going to fall on them. (We said): "Hold firmly to what We have given you (Tawrah), and remember that which is therein (act on its commandments), so that you may fear Allah and obey Him.")(7:171).

**Hold firmly to what We have given you, and observe its teachings.**

Mujahid said that the Ayah commanded, "Strictly adhere to it. (and remember that which is therein) means, "Read the Tawrah and implement it. "Hold fast to that which We have given you, and remember that which is therein so that you may acquire Taqwa Then after that you turned away. (Hold fast that which We have given you) comply with what We have given of the scripture in earnestness and diligence, (and remember that which is therein) of reward and chastisement, and recollect what is in it of the lawful and unlawful, (that ye may ward off (evil) in order that you may ward off Allah's wrath and torment and so that you may obey Him. He raised the mountain over you, inspiring awe and warning you against breaking the contract, commanding you to take what He had revealed to you of the Torah seriously and carefully, not taking it for granted or being lazy about it. He told you to remember and reflect upon it, so that you might be careful about what you earn from Allah. To have faith is to make a contract with God that one will live and die in accordance with His will. If man keeps his word, he will be granted God’s eternal blessings. But if he turns away from his commitment, he is in grave danger of being cast into hell-fire, never to emerge again. Everyone who binds himself to the contract of faith should live in the fear of breaking his religious vows, thereby bringing catastrophe down upon himself. Sometimes those entrusted with the law of God go astray by contradicting it in practice, while finding words to make it appear that they are following it to the letter. The Israelites, for instance, were commanded to keep holy the Sabbath day, and refrain from worldly pursuits on that day. But they violated it and went about their work on the Sabbath as on any other day. Furthermore, they sought to justify their actions and made out that what they were doing conformed to the will of God.

**Force, and what the verse is not about.**

The Holy Qur'an says in another place that force should not be used to make a man change his religion, while in the present instance it appears that force is being used. But, in fact, force is not being used to make the Israelites change their religion, for they had already accepted Sayyidna Musa as a prophet of Allah, and willingly made a covenant with Allah that they would act upon the Book of Allah, if one was given to them. So, they now stand as rebels, and are being threatened with dire punishment for persisting in their rebellion. This is exactly how even a secular state deals with rebels, and how it adopts towards them an attitude quite different from that towards aliens or enemies, for it leaves only two ways open to the rebel -- either to submit himself, or to lose his life. That is why it is only an apostate (Murtadd) who is, according to the Islamic Shari ah, condemned to capital punishment, and not an outright disbeliever. Moreover, the Israelites were being threatened with death as criminals and offenders against the law which they acknowledged to be the divine law, but which they refused to obey.

**A covenant with all who are responsible, and the respite given.**

He made a covenant with all responsible beings and some responded willingly because He made Himself known to them and they declared His unity fa-waḥḥadūhu. Other people responded unwill ingly because He veiled them so they did not want to recognize Him fa-jaḥadūhu. If not for His decree in grant ing respite and His forbearance through acts of grace He would punish you without delay and cause a great misfortune to descend upon you and your deeds would be entirely a loss.

64.text:
The verse is short and it does two things, and the two are the turning and the holding back. "Yet you turned away afterwards" is the first, and the afterwards is what gives the sentence its weight, since the turning is not a falling short at the moment of the covenant but a leaving of it once the mountain had gone and the pledge had been taken, so the word puts the turning at a distance from the event that produced it. "Had it not been for Allah's grace and mercy upon you" is the second thing, and it is put as a condition that did not happen, the grace and the mercy being named together as the reason the turning did not end in what it deserved. Two names are used and not one, and the pair covers both the withholding of the punishment and the giving of what came after it, so the verse is not only about being spared but about being spared and then given something. "you would have certainly been of the losers" is what the condition keeps off, and the loss is named in the general form rather than as one particular punishment, which leaves it covering this life and the next, and leaves the breach of the covenant as the ground of it.

**Yet you turned away afterwards.**

Then you turned away thereafter and but for God’s bounty and His mercy towards you you would have been among the losers there is no commentary on this verse. (Then, even after that, you turned away) you turned your back on the covenant, (and if it had not been for the grace of Allah upon you) by deferring His punishment (and His mercy) by sending Muhammad ﷺ to you (you had been among the losers) you would have among the duped who are exposed to Allah's punishment. (Then after that you turned away. Had it not been for the grace of Allah) means, "Yet, after the firm pledge that you gave, you still deviated and broke your pledge";. Then you turned away thereafter that is you returned to disobedience after witnessing the signs with your own eyes. Yet after making a firm promise, you broke the contract and rebelled.

**Had it not been for Allah's grace and mercy.**

(Had it not been for the grace and mercy of Allah upon you), meaning, by forgiving you and by sending the Prophets and Messengers to you,. If it had not been for Allah’s favour in His tolerance towards you, and His mercy, accepting when you asked for forgiveness, then you would be among the losers because of your turning away and rebellion. But Allah, in His mercy, spared them in so far as physical life is concerned, although they will have to pay for their treason in the other world. The other is special, and pertains to believers alone -- it will manifest itself particularly in the other world in the shape of salvation and closeness to Allah. In this verse, Allah asks them to realize that it is in His mercy alone that he has not, in spite of their treason, sent down on them the kind of catastrophic punishment in this world as used to descend on the other infidels and traitors who have gone before. Since a number of authentic ahadith declare that it is the barakah of the Holy Prophet that catastrophic punishments no longer descend on any people, some commentators have identified this particular mercy and grace of Allah with the sending down of Muhammad as a Prophet and Messenger of Allah. If not for His decree in grant ing respite and His forbearance through acts of grace He would punish you without delay and cause a great misfortune to descend upon you and your deeds would be entirely a loss.

**The breach of the covenant, and the punishment held back.**

(Indeed you would have been among the losers) meaning, in this life and the Hereafter due to their breach of the covenant. The Israelites went against the Covenant they had made with Allah. The sin was so grave that one could have expected utter destruction and ruin to descend on them as a punishment. Since having faith in him is also a part of the Covenant, these Jews too have been included among those who had been guilty of infringement. To have faith is to make a contract with God that one will live and die in accordance with His will. But if he turns away from his commitment, he is in grave danger of being cast into hell-fire, never to emerge again. Everyone who binds himself to the contract of faith should live in the fear of breaking his religious vows, thereby bringing catastrophe down upon himself.

65.text:
The verse turns from the general rule of the last one to a single thing that happened, and it turns by putting the people in mind of it. "You are already aware of those of you who broke the Sabbath" opens on knowing rather than on being told, and the awareness is named as something they already have, so the verse is not handing them a story but bringing back one they hold, and the breaking is put as a breaking of the day itself and not of a command about the day. The words of you are what make it theirs, since the people addressed are the ones whose ancestors did the thing, and the verse keeps the doing inside the same house rather than setting it at a distance. "We said to them" is the answer, and it is given as a speech and not as an event, so what follows is not a description of a change but the wording of it. "Be disgraced apes" is that wording, and it is a command in the shape of a making, the two words being the state they are put in and the name of what they are put into, and the disgrace is joined to the change so that the shape is not the whole of the punishment.

**Those of you who broke the Sabbath.**

And verily wa-la-qad the lām is for oaths you know that there were those among you who transgressed violated the Sabbath by fishing when We had forbidden you to do so — these were the inhabitants of Eilat — and We said to them ‘Be apes despised!’ rejected and they became so they died three days later. (And ye know) you indeed know and heard about the punishment (of those of you who broke) who have taken the covenant (the Sabbath) the day of Saturday and this at the time of David ﷺ (how We said unto them: Be ye apes, despised and hated!) turned into humiliated and base apes. You know well the story of your ancestors, who prepared to fish on the Sabbath when they were not allowed to do so, and did so through trickery. And verily you know that there were those among you who transgressed the Sabbath and We said to them Be apes despised! The Israelites, for instance, were commanded to keep holy the Sabbath day, and refrain from worldly pursuits on that day. Sometimes those entrusted with the law of God go astray by contradicting it in practice, while finding words to make it appear that they are following it to the letter. They began using deceitful means to avoid honoring the Sabbath by placing nets, ropes and artificial pools of water for the purpose of fishing before the Sabbath.

**The town by the sea, and the trickery used in it.**

(And ask them (O Muhammad) about the town that was by the sea; when they transgressed in the matter of the Sabbath (i.e. Saturday): when their fish came to them openly on the Sabbath day, and did not come to them on the day they had no Sabbath. Thus We made a trial of them, for they used to rebel (disobey Allah).)(7:163) They set up nets in preparation for the Sabbath so Allah made them into monkeys, rejected and cast out, because of their trickery. The transgression on the part of the Jews which the verse speaks of, and which drew upon them such dreadful punishment, was not a clear and explicit infringement of divine law, but the use of certain "tricks" which necessarily involved the negation of the divine commandment. That is why those who practiced such "stratagems" were considered to be disobedient and rebellious, and subjected to dire punishment.

**Be apes, despised.**

(We said to them: "Be you monkeys, despised and rejected") means, "Allah changed their bodies into those of monkeys and swines. Ibn Abi Hatim recorded that Ibn 'Abbas said, "Those who violated the sanctity of the Sabbath were turned into monkeys, then they perished without offspring. " Ad-Dahhak said that Ibn 'Abbas said, "Allah turned them into monkeys because of their sins. This audacity incurred God’s displeasure and they were turned into apes. The metamorphosis maskh of this community occurred in their hearts. Because of their violation of the covenant and rejection of the limit [imposed by God] the community was punished through the metamorphosis of their hearts and the alteration of their states. [God] most high said And We shall confound their hearts and their eyes; just as they did not believe the first time [6:110]. The punishments of hearts are far worse than the punishments of the bodily selves. According to a hadith reported by Imam Muslim from the blessed Companion Abdullah ibn Masud some people asked the Holy Prophet whether the apes and the swine were the descendants of the metamorphosed Jews. The Holy Prophet reminded them that apes and swine existed in the world even before, and said that when Allah sends down this particular kind of punishment on a people, the race comes to an end with this, and there is no further breeding.24. Some 'modernizing' Muslims have tried to explain away this metamorphosis by suggesting that these disobedient Jews did not actually and physically turn into beasts, but that the change was only psychological in so far as they acquired the evil characteristics of apes and swine. For, even before the punishment fell on them, these Jews had been displaying the moral and psychological traits of beasts: the greed of swine and the craftiness of apes.

66.text:
What the last verse did to a people, this one makes into a thing that stays. "So We made their fate an example to present and future generations" takes the punishment out of the moment it fell in and puts it where it can be looked at, and the making is named as a making rather than as a leaving, so the example is something set up and not merely something that happened and was remembered. The two generations are the ones in front of it and the ones behind it, and the wording covers both directions of time, which is why the fate is not a warning to the people who came after only but a thing fixed in the middle of a line that runs both ways. "and a lesson to the God-fearing" puts a second use beside the first, and the second is not the same as the first, since an example is what the fate is and a lesson is what it gives, and the giving is turned towards one group rather than towards all who hear of it. The group named is the God-fearing, which puts the lesson in the hands of the people who are already keeping the limits, so the verse is not threatening them with the fate of the village but arming them against the way the village got there, the ruses and the pretences that made the sin look like obedience.

**An example to present and future generations.**

So We made this punishment an example for those in front of it and those behind it, and a lesson for Al-Muttaqin (the pious. (And We made it) turning them into apes (an example) we subjected them to a chastisement (to their own) for the sins they had committed before, made them a lesson (to succeeding generations) in order that they do not follow their example (and admonition to the God-fearing) and a counsel and warning to those who fear Allah, i.e. And We made it an exemplary punishment for all the former times and for the latter and an admonition to those who fear. Therefore, Allah made them an example for those who lived during their time as well as a reminder for those to come, by preserving their story.

**A lesson to those who fear.**

And We made it this punishment an exemplary punishment a lesson to dissuade others from doing what they did; for all the former times and for the latter that is for the people of that time or those that came later; and an admonition to such as who fear God these are singled out for mention here because they in contrast to others are the ones who benefit thereby. He made it a reminder for those mindful of Allah, who are careful of facing the consequences of their actions in the life to come, and are mindful of Allah’s repayment for those who transgress the limits. For the disobedient, it served as a 'deterrent', an example and a warning, which persuaded them to repent of their disobedience. For the obedient, it was a lesson and a reminder that they should be steadfast in their obedience. Hence, those who have Taqwa should be aware of their evil behavior, so that what occurred to this village does not befall them as well. Those who play games with divine law, should fear being deprived of their human dignity, and being brought down to the level of animals. The same is the case with everyone who embraces true faith. Thus the states of those who were tried by abandonment muniya bi-l hijrān and branded with disappointment wusima bi-l-khidhlān became a lesson-to look at what happened to them is to choke on grief. The one who is reduced to misery after having had status becomes an object of scorn before every ignoble person. This is what remains for those who have been brought low after [experiencing] the wrath of kings and [being] shunned by chieftains:

**The punishment of the village, and the ruses behind it.**

(So We made this punishment an example) means, Allah made the people of this village, who violated the sanctity of the Sabbath,. Allah made this village, which had transgressed the limits, an example to the surrounding villages, and an example to those who came after it, so that they would not do the same and deserve the same fate. This Ayah means, "The torment and punishment that this village suffered was a result of indulging in Allah's prohibitions and their deceit. This is why their punishment was compatible with their crime. We have been saying that the Jews who were changed into apes had used certain ruses or pretences to justify their sin in their own eyes. For example, bartering a kilo of good dates for two kilos of bad dates is, according to the Shari'ah, a kind of usury. So, they have complete certitude with regard to Darwin's speculation, that the apes evolved into man, although no verifiable data has yet been gathered to support the contention; but when it comes to the statement in the Holy Qur'an that men were changed into apes, they look askance at it, although this kind of change is rationally and logically as possible as the other.

67.text:
The story the last verses were leading to begins here, and it begins with a command that makes no sense to the people it is given to. "And remember when Moses said to his people" puts the scene in the same frame as the verses before it, a thing to be remembered and not a thing being argued, and the people named are his people, the same group the covenant was taken from and the same group that turned away after it. "Allah commands you to sacrifice a cow, They replied, Are you mocking us" gives the command and the answer to it in one breath, and the oddity of the command is the point of everything that follows, since a cow is not what a people asking for a killer would be given, and the naming of the animal without a reason for it is what makes the asking that comes next possible. The command is put as coming from Allah and not as a judgement of Moses, which is why the answer that follows is not a refusal of Moses but a doubt about whether he is serious, and the doubt takes the command as a joke rather than as a test, so the question is not about the cow but about the standing of the one who gave it, and the mockery named is the mockery of a prophet by the people he is sent to. "Are you mocking us, Moses responded, I seek refuge in Allah from acting foolishly" carries the question into the reply, and the reply is not a denial but a taking of cover, the foolishness being put as a thing he asks to be kept from rather than as a thing he is charged with, so the answer turns the charge back on itself without naming anyone. What the verse leaves standing is the gap between the command and the reason for it, and the rest of the passage is the people asking that gap to be closed, one question at a time, until the cow they have to find is a single animal in a single hand. The killing that started it is not named in the verse, and the reason for the command is not given in it either, so the reader is put where the people were, holding an order with no visible ground under it, and what comes next is the killing, the asking, and the price the asking ended at.

**When one of them was killed, and the killer was not known.**

And mention when Moses said to his people when one among them was killed and the killer was not known and so they asked Moses to pray to God to reveal the killer which he did; ‘God commands you to sacrifice a cow’. Ibn Abi Hatim recorded 'Ubaydah As-Salmani saying, "There was a man from among the Children of Israel who was impotent. He had substantial wealth, and only a nephew who would inherit from him. So his nephew killed him and moved his body at night, placing it at the doorstep of a certain man. The next morning, the nephew cried out for revenge, and the people took up their weapons and almost fought each other. The wise men among them said, 'Why would you kill each other, while the Messenger of Allah is still among you?' So they went to Musa and mentioned the matter to him and Musa said,. Remember how I blessed you with miracle of the cow that was the means for discovering the identity of the murderer, when the murdered man was brought back to life.'. According to Mirqat, a commentary on Mishkat, a man among the Israelites wanted to marry a girl, but her father refused. The suitor was so incensed that he killed the father, and disappeared. Anyhow, the Israelites requested Sayyidna Musa to tell them how to trace the culprit. It is mentioned in Ma alim al-tanzil which says on the authority of Kalbi that Allah had not yet sent down any injunction with regard to man-slaughter. If it was so, this shows that the incident happened before the Torah was revealed.

**Allah commands you to sacrifice a cow.**

"Verily, Allah commands you that you slaughter a cow. ("Verily, Allah commands you that you slaughter a cow." They said, "Do you make fun of us?" He said, "I take Allah's refuge from being among Al-Jahilin (the ignorant or the foolish)." Allah then mentions the story of the cow, saying: (And when Moses said unto his people: Lo! Allah commandeth you that ye sacrifice a cow) any cow, (they said: Dost thou make game of us?) are you really mocking us? From the stories of your ancestors, remember what happened between them and Moses ﷺ when he told them that Allah had instructed them to slaughter a cow. Under the commandment of Allah, he asked them to sacrifice a cow. They said ‘Do you take us in mockery?’ that is making fun of us when you answer us like this?

**I take refuge from being among the ignorant and the foolish.**

He said ‘I take refuge with I seek defence with God lest I should be one of the ignorant’ one of those who indulge in mockery. " He said, "I take Allah's refuge from being among Al-Jahilin (the ignorant or the foolish). Moses (answered: Allah forbid that I should be among the foolish!) God forbid that I ever mock the believers. ’ Moses replied that he asked for Allah’s protection from being one of the ignorant people, who lied about Allah, and made fun of other people. Instead of hurrying to do so, they said, stubbornly, ‘Are you making fun of us? As was their regular habit, they started raising all kinds of doubts and objections, of which the next verses give us the details.

**The dispute, and what it cost to slaughter the cow.**

"Had they not disputed, it would have been sufficient for them to slaughter any cow. However, they disputed, and the matter was made more difficult for them, until they ended up looking for the specific cow that they were later ordered to slaughter. They found the designated cow with a man, only who owned that cow. I will only sell it for its skin's fill of gold.' So they paid the cow's fill of its skin in gold, slaughtered it and touched the dead man with a part of it. He stood up, and they asked him, 'Who killed you?' He said, 'That man,' and pointed to his nephew. He died again, and his nephew was not allowed to inherit him. Thereafter, whoever committed murder for the purpose of gaining inheritance was not allowed to inherit.

**The story of the cow in these verses, read as an allusion.**

" This story of the cow of the Children of Israel in these verses and the mention of its attributes is one of the subtle points of wisdom and exalted pearls of the Qur'an. The Qur'an itself is the all-encom passing ocean. Many are the kingly pearls and night-brightening gems found in the ocean's depths. You should read everything that the Exalted Lord said about the cow of the Children of Israel as an allusion to your own attributes. Then you will reach the station of worthiness to dive into this ocean and He will give you access to its deposited wonders and unseen pearls. Altogether the attributes that He clarified in these verses are three: first, neither old nor virgin [2:68]; second, golden, bright her color [2:69]; third, not abased to plow the earth [2:71]. He says it should not be broken down and old, nor newly born and immature. Do you not see that revelation reached MuṣṬafā when he was not a newly born youngster, nor had his days reached the worst state of life [16:70]? If there had been a state more complete, revelation would have reached him at its time. Whenever desire for God pairs itself with the intoxication of youth, there is fear of the high waymen. It is rare that a youngster in his new desire remains secure from the highwaymen. This is why MuṣṬafā said, "Your Lord marvels at a young man who has no youthful fervor.

68.text:
The command of the last verse is answered here not by an act but by a question, and the question is the first of three. "They said, Call upon your Lord to clarify for us what type of cow it should be, He replied, Allah says, The cow should neither be old nor young but in between. So do as you are commanded" is the whole of the exchange, and the asking in it is put as directed through Moses and not to him, with the Lord named as your Lord and not as our Lord, which is the same distance the earlier verses kept marking, the people treating the prophet as a go-between with someone else's God. What they ask for is a clarification, so the command is not refused but kept waiting, and the waiting is what makes the asking a way of not doing. The answer comes back in the same form as the command, a speech from Allah passed on without addition, and it is a limit on both sides with a middle kept between them, so the cow is defined by what it is not and then by the place it has between the two. The two sides named are the two ends of a life, the old and the young, and the middle kept between them is the point of strength, which is why the answer is an age and not a colour or a mark, and why the descriptions that come after it are asked for by the people rather than given at the start. The middle named here is not a compromise between two goods but the point at which the animal is at its strength, so the limit given is a limit on usefulness and not on appearance, and the appearance is what the asking goes on to. The command repeated at the end is what keeps the verse from being a description only, since a description that is not followed by doing leaves the asking where it started. The two limits given are limits on the age of the animal and not on its looks or its work, so the description is still a description of a kind and not of a single cow, and the kind is wide enough that any cow answering it would do, which is the point the answer keeps and the people keep missing. What the verse is doing is holding the command in front of them a second time, in the same words, with one narrowing added to it, and the narrowing is the smallest one that can be made without naming an animal, so the doing asked for at the end is still within the reach of anyone who has a cow. The middle between the two ages is where an animal is at its strength and its usefulness, and the verse asks for that middle rather than for an extreme on either side, which is a way of asking for what is ordinary and available and not for what is rare. The reply closes with the command repeated, and the repeating is the turning in it, since the answer to the asking is not a new description only but the same order given again, with the doing put after the clarifying so that the clarifying cannot become a substitute for the act. The verse is the middle of a pattern in which every asking narrows the thing asked for and makes it harder to find, and the narrowing is not a punishment sent from outside but the shape the command takes once it is answered with questions.

**Call upon your Lord to clarify for us what type it should be.**

But when they realised that he was being serious They said ‘Pray to your Lord for us that He may make clear to us what she may be’ its true nature He Moses said ‘He God says she is a cow neither old nor virgin that is young middling between the two in terms of age; so do what you have been commanded’ by way of sacrificing it. (Call upon your Lord for us that He may make plain to us what it is!), meaning, "What is this cow and what is its description? When they realised he was truthful, (They said: Pray for us unto your Lord That He make clear to us what she is) whether the cow is large or small. They asked Moses to call on his Lord to clarify what the cow they had been told to sacrifice was like.

**A cow neither old nor young, but between the two.**

(He says, 'Verily, it is a cow neither too old nor too young'), meaning, that it is neither old nor below the age of breeding. Rather, she was at the age when the cow is strongest and fittest. (Moses answered: Lo! He saith, Verily she is a cow neither old nor immature; (she is) between the two conditions) neither large nor small; (so do that which ye are commanded) and ask no further questions. She is a cow neither old nor virgin middling between the two... [2:68] it meant she would be neither young nor aged but some where between the two. The allusion is to the fact that one who is suited for this path Ṭarīqa is one who is neither attracted by the impetuosity of youth and its drunkenness nor paralyzed by the weakness and frailty of old age. Rather he is alert; he has regained consciousness from his drunkenness yet retains some of the vigor of his youth.

**So do as you are commanded.**

These Verses show how the Israelites were disposed to disobedience, and how this inclination expressed itself in different forms. The Hadith says that if these people had obeyed Allah's commandment without raising so many doubts and asking unnecessary questions, such strict condition would not have been imposed on them, and the sacrifice of any cow whatsoever would have been accepted. This is why when they were stubborn, Allah made the decisions difficult for them. Had they slaughtered a cow, any cow, it would have been sufficient for them, as Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ubaydah have said. Instead, they made the matter difficult, and this is why Allah made it even more difficult for them. (So they slaughtered it though they were near to not doing it) means, "They did not want to slaughter it." This part of the Qur'an criticized the Jews for their behavior, because their only goal was to be stubborn, and this is why they nearly did not slaughter the cow. Also, 'Ubaydah, Mujahid, Wahb bin Munabbih, Abu Al-'Aliyah and 'Abdur-Rahman bin Zayd bin Aslam said, "The Jews bought the cow with a large amount of money. The Stubbornness of the Jews regarding the Cow; Allah made the Matter difficult for Them. It was obligatory for them to execute the command directly but they wasted time with external appearances imagining that they had the leisure to linger in their digression from the obligation of the covenant. So their misery was doubled and the ignominy they had been warned about overtook them.

**Further questions, and the descriptions asked for.**

Allah mentioned the stubbornness of the Children of Israel and the many unnecessary questions they asked their Messengers. This means that even after all the questions and answers about the cow's description, the Jews were still reluctant to slaughter the cow. (Verily, to us all cows are alike) this means, that since cows are plentiful, then describe this cow for us further,. (And surely, if Allah wills) and if you further describe it to us,. And surely, if Allah wills, we will be guided.

69.text:
The third asking is about colour, and the answer is the shortest of the three. "They said, Call upon your Lord to specify for us its colour, He replied, Allah says, It should be a bright yellow cow—pleasant to see" carries the whole exchange, and the asking in it is put in the same words as the two before it, your Lord and make clear, so nothing in the form of the question has changed since the first round. What has changed is the thing asked about, since the age of the cow was a matter of what it is and its colour is a matter of how it looks, and the move from the one to the other is the move the passage is about. "It should be a bright yellow cow" answers with a single colour and a single quality of it, the brightness being part of the colour and not a second mark added to it, so the answer narrows the search without describing an animal that could not be found. "pleasant to see" is the last word of the answer and the only one of them that is not a limit, since it puts the cow in front of the eyes of the people looking for it and gives what the looking will find, and it is the one part of the description that is about the cow as seen rather than as chosen.

**Call upon your Lord to make clear its colour.**

They continued debating and being stubborn, telling Moses ﷺ to call on his Lord to make clear to them the colour of the cow. (They said: Pray for us unto your Lord that He make clear to us of what colour she is) what colour the cow is. They said ‘Pray to your Lord for us that He make clear to us what her colour may be’ He said ‘He says she shall be a golden cow bright in colour that is of a very intense yellow gladdening to beholders its beauty will please those that look at it. They said Pray to your Lord for us that He make clear to us what she may be; the cows are all alike to us; and if God wills we shall then be guided.

**A bright yellow cow, pleasant to see.**

Moses told them that Allah said that it was a yellow cow, with a very strong colour, which was pleasing to everyone who saw it. ((Moses) answered: Lo! He saith: Surely she is a yellow cow) her hoofs and horns are yellow while her body is black. (Bright is her colour) her colour is light, (gladdening beholders) pleasing those who look at her. (bright in its colour) "A deep yellowish white." " This is also the opinion of Abu Al-'Aliyah and Ar-Rabi'. (pleasing the beholder) meaning, that it pleases those who see it. Or, it might be that the cow was so yellow that it appeared blackish or reddish in color. Furthermore, Wahb bin Munabbih said, "If you look at the cow's skin, you will think that the sun's rays radiate through its skin. This is also the opinion of Abu Al-'Aliyah, Qatadah and Ar-Rabi' bin Anas. " The modern version of the Tawrah mentions that the cow in the Ayah was red, but this is an error.

**The simplicity of the religion lost, and the lesson in it.**

Another mistake that the Israelites had made was to destroy the simplicity of divine religion by involving themselves in complicated theological wrangling. They had to learn to interpret God’s will in a straightforward manner and obey it immediately. This was another lesson that was taught under the pretext of this murder case: hair-splitting to define the exact scope of divine edicts will only make things difficult for everyone; additional conditions will only complicate the carrying out of what had originally been a simple commandment. These Verses show how the Israelites were disposed to disobedience, and how this inclination expressed itself in different forms. The Hadith says that if these people had obeyed Allah's commandment without raising so many doubts and asking unnecessary questions, such strict condition would not have been imposed on them, and the sacrifice of any cow whatsoever would have been accepted.

**What the eyes perceive, and what is seen of God.**

Just as her [bright] color would have been perceived by the eyes the allu sion here is to those of the people of the story ahl al-qiṣṣa whose witnessing overwhelms the hearts [of others] because of that which is clothed with the garment of invincibility jabarūt and made to rise from the witness of the unseen. One notices that someone like this is oblivious to human states and is overtaken by the remembrance of the Real. The friends of God are those who when they are seen God is remembered.

70.text:
The asking goes on, and this verse is the third round of it. "Again they said, Call upon your Lord so that He may make clear to us which cow, for all cows look the same to us. Then, Allah willing, we will be guided to the right one" is the whole of their speech, and the word again at the front of it is the only mark the verse gives of how many times this has now happened, so the repetition is put in the opening word and not in a comment on it. The asking keeps the same shape as the two before it, your Lord and make clear, and the shape is what makes the three rounds one thing rather than three questions, since in each of them the people put themselves at a distance from the command and ask for the distance to be closed by an answer. What is new here is the reason given for the asking, and the reason is that all cows look the same to us, which is not a doubt about the command but a claim about the world, so the asking has moved from what the cow is to whether it can be picked out at all. The answer to that claim is not given in the verse, and the verse leaves the matter where the first round left it, with the description standing and the finding of it not yet attempted. The narrowing is worth marking, because the first asking was about what the cow is, the second was answered with an age, the third with a colour, and this one asks which of them, so the questions have run from the kind to the single animal, and the single animal is the one thing a description cannot give. The claim of sameness is what makes the asking endless, since if every cow looks like every other then no description can end the search, and the search can only be ended by a cow being pointed at, which is not what a description does. That is why the answer to this round is not another mark on the animal but the same command given again, and why the guidance named at the end is guidance to a particular cow rather than to a rule. "Then, Allah willing, we will be guided to the right one" is the last part, and it is the first time in the passage that the people put a thing in the hands of Allah rather than in the hands of Moses, since the willing named is his and not theirs, and the guidance asked for is guidance to the cow and not to the command. The proviso is what the verse turns on, and the hadīth that goes with these words is that had they not been uttered the thing would never have been made clear to them, so the small clause at the end of the asking is the part of it that was accepted, and the three rounds of questions before it are the part that was not. What is left after the verse is a people who have asked three times and done nothing, and an animal now described in a way that only one of them can answer.

**Call upon your Lord to make clear which cow, for all cows are alike.**

They said ‘Pray to your Lord for us that He make clear to us what she may be does it graze freely or is it used in labour?; the cows that is the species described in the way mentioned are all alike to us because there are many of them and we have not been able to find the one sought after; and if God wills we shall then be guided’ to it. They continued in their stubbornness, telling Moses to ask Allah to further clarify the nature of the cow. (Verily, to us all cows are alike) this means, that since cows are plentiful, then describe this cow for us further,. (And surely, if Allah wills) and if you further describe it to us,.

**Then, Allah willing, we will be guided.**

(Lo! Cows are much alike to us) we cannot distinguish much between cows; (and lo! If Allah wills, we may be led rightfully) to its fitting description; as it is said that this means: we may be led to the murder of 'Amil. They said that there were many cows fitting the description, and they could not therefore identify it, insisting that they would then, if Allah willed, be guided to the right cow for sacrifice. In one hadīth it is reported ‘Had they not uttered the proviso inshā’a Llāh it would never have been made clear to them’. The Hadith says that if these people had obeyed Allah's commandment without raising so many doubts and asking unnecessary questions, such strict condition would not have been imposed on them, and the sacrifice of any cow whatsoever would have been accepted.

**The stubbornness, and the matter made difficult.**

Allah mentioned the stubbornness of the Children of Israel and the many unnecessary questions they asked their Messengers. Instead, they made the matter difficult, and this is why Allah made it even more difficult for them. This means that even after all the questions and answers about the cow's description, the Jews were still reluctant to slaughter the cow. This part of the Qur'an criticized the Jews for their behavior, because their only goal was to be stubborn, and this is why they nearly did not slaughter the cow. The Stubbornness of the Jews regarding the Cow; Allah made the Matter difficult for Them. These Verses show how the Israelites were disposed to disobedience, and how this inclination expressed itself in different forms. This was another lesson that was taught under the pretext of this murder case: hair-splitting to define the exact scope of divine edicts will only make things difficult for everyone; additional conditions will only complicate the carrying out of what had originally been a simple commandment. This is why when they were stubborn, Allah made the decisions difficult for them. Also, 'Ubaydah, Mujahid, Wahb bin Munabbih, Abu Al-'Aliyah and 'Abdur-Rahman bin Zayd bin Aslam said, "The Jews bought the cow with a large amount of money. (He says, 'Verily, it is a cow neither too old nor too young'), meaning, that it is neither old nor below the age of breeding. (But (it is) between the two conditions) means, "Neither old nor young. " This is also the opinion of Abu Al-'Aliyah and Ar-Rabi'.

71.text:
The description ends here, and the verse ends with the animal dead. "He replied, Allah says, It should have been used neither to till the soil nor water the fields; wholesome and without blemish. They said, Now you have come with the truth. Yet they still slaughtered it hesitantly" is the whole of the exchange, and it is the only one of the rounds that carries both the answer and what the people did about it. The answer has two halves in it, and the halves are of different kinds. The first is a pair of negations, neither to till the soil nor water the fields, and what it takes away from the cow is work, so the animal asked for is one that has not been used, and the two forms of work named are the two a cow in that land was kept for, the plough and the watering of the fields. The second half is a pair of affirmations, wholesome and without blemish, and the two words are not the same thing, since wholesomeness is the soundness of the animal as a whole and the absence of blemish is the absence of a mark on it, so the first is what the cow is and the second is what is not on it.
